newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FEATURE-Australia gold miner ignores Busang woes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Australia gold miner ignores Busang woes.

text.p: While shareholders in Bre-X Minerals await the next word on how much -- or little -- gold exists in Indonesia's Busang prospect, an Australian miner is spending millions of dollars to extend its own nearby lode.

Aurora Gold Ltd is sinking half its annual budget of US$12-$13 million into expanding its Mt Muro mine in East Kalimantan province, a 500 sq km (188 square mile) area of dense forest populated chiefly by Dayak people, Aurora managing director Ian Burston told Reuters.
Mt Muro already yields 180,000 ounces of gold and three million ounces of silver a year at costs well below the going rate for both metals.
But Burston says there is plenty more gold in East Kalimantan on the Indonesian side of Borneo island.
Aurora geologists are busy clearing new sections of the dense terrain around the existing mine with an eye toward finding more of the precious metal.
It is no easy task given the mine's surroundings.
AN INHOSPITABLE ENVIRONMENT
One geologist narrowly escaped an attack last week by a cobra while doing field work, a not uncommon incident in Borneo, said an Aurora employee.

Aurora would also like to make its own explosives at the mine instead of shouldering the cost of transporting emulsions 600 km (370 miles) up the Barito River, an idea meeting only a lukewarm reception by the government.

Meanwhile, machine gun-wielding government forces acting as a resident security force at the mine are also on call to shift an increasing number of illegal independent miners who covertly set up ad-hoc camps within the Mt Muro site.

The often brazen independents cost Aurora A$1 million ($776,000) in lost revenue each year and their extraction methods pose an environmental threat to the region's fragile river system, Burston said.
But the independents also confirm what Burston said is becoming increasingly apparent -- there is more gold to be found in East Kalimantan,
"With two or three fellows swinging machetes, we can put a survey line followed by another half-dozen guys backpacking a drilling unit in," Burston said.
"Gold mining is about exploration and resources and reserves and bringing it into production," he said.
"But the first question asked is always what do you have next ... There's an element of the blue sky in there."
By digging deeper at Mt Muro and testing new ground, Aurora hopes to lift gold reserves by one million ounces in three years, Burston said.
It is an achievable yet "ambitious" goal, he said, with some 1,000 employees, mostly Dayak people, mining and studying the mineral-rich epithermal deposits that form Mt Muro.
Still, the figure is far less than the 71 million ounces in gold reserves Canada's Bre-X previously estimated was contained in the Busang deposit.
The Bre-X claim is now being investigated by the Indonesian government and potential U.S. joint venture partner Freeport McMoran Copper and Gold Inc.
On March 26 both Bre-X and Freeport said the claim may have been overstated.
The geologist credited with helping discover Busang, Michael de Guzman, plunged to his death from a helicopter over the Borneo jungle while on his way to a meeting with Freeport geologists.
EXPANSION PLANNED
Some 280 km (175 miles) south of Busang at Mt Muro, geologists are readying an update of the gold resource for a shareholders report later this month.

A decision is also due soon on whether to proceed with development of the Toka Tindung mine in Sulawesi, an Indonesian island to the east of Borneo, at an initial rate of 80,000 ounces a year, Burston said.
"I want to be making gold there by the end of next year," Burston said.
Bre-X shareholders are waiting for word on the results of tests of ore samples from Busang being conducted by Freeport and others in the hopes they will point to some gold.

Bre-X's rags-to-riches ascent on the Toronto Stock Exchange ended on March 27 when the stock lost 84 percent of its value in the first 30 minutes of trading. The volume of trading in Bre-X was so great it knocked out the exchange's computer system.
Senior Freeport geologist David Potter has been assigned to remove uncertainties over just how much gold is contained in the Busang deposit.
Approached in a restaurant in the port city of Balikpapan in East Kalimantan, Potter declined to be interviewed by Reuters and refused to comment on Busang.

Aurora stock, traded on the Australian Stock Exchange, has also taken a licking over the Busang debacle. Stockbrokers cited a knock-on effect brought on by nervous investors which has punished some miners operating in Indonesia.
"The stock fell to a low of around A$2 ($1.54) a share from a recent high of about A$2.60 ($2.00)," Burston said.
Aurora shares were last trading on Tuesday at A$2.00.
Burston said he did not like to see his company's stock price go down, although he says the Bre-X effect could have been worse.
"Fortunately, the Australian investor community is quite sophisticated and can recognise that we operate a real mine with strong exploration potential," Burston said.
